MUQATIL:78:11-16/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:78:11-16/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:78:11-16/r5.claim: The rain brings forth grain, including wheat, barley, and sesame, and plants such as wild trees and grass that grow in open country and renew annually.

NAHHAS:v5p127/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p127/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p127/r1.claim: Ḥabb is any grain with a husk; nabāt is grass, fodder, and similar growth.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r1.speaker: الضحاك
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r1.claim: Grain means the seed in the husk that is harvested, while vegetation means pasture grass for grazing.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r2.speaker: عكرمة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r2.claim: Another explanation is that grain means pearls and vegetation means grass; Ikrima says every rain drop produces grass on land or a pearl in the sea.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p184/r3.claim: Alternatively, grain means what people sow and vegetation what they did not sow.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p124/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p124/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p124/r1.claim: The water brings forth grain that people eat and vegetation that livestock eat.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p313#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p313#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p313#2/r1.claim: The rain brings out grains people eat and plants the livestock eat.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p425/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p425/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p425/r1.claim: حب refers to grains useful as food for animals, while نبات is grass used fresh by people or animals; the verse names both kinds of benefit.

TABRISI:78:2-16/r19.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:78:2-16/r19.speaker: author
TABRISI:78:2-16/r19.claim: The water brings out grain enclosed in crop husks and vegetation such as herbage and plants, encompassing earth's produce.

TABRISI:78:2-16/r20.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:78:2-16/r20.speaker: author
TABRISI:78:2-16/r20.claim: Another interpretation assigns grain to what people eat and vegetation to what livestock eat.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r1.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r1.claim: The grain is food for people; the plants are growth eaten by people and livestock.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r2.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r2.claim: Everything harvested is grain, while pasture eaten by livestock is called vegetation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r3.speaker: عكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#4/r3.claim: Alternatively, grain means pearls and vegetation means grass; every rain from heaven grows pearls in the sea and grass on land.

RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r5.claim: All terrestrial growth falls into three exhaustive classes: grain with husks, grasses without husks or stems, and trees that form gardens; 20:54 names the first two.

RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r6.claim: Grain comes first because it is basic food, plants next because animals need them, and orchards last because fruit is less essential.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r9.claim: The water brings forth grains such as wheat and barley and vegetation such as fodder eaten by animals.

BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r3.claim: Rain brings out grain for human food and vegetation for livestock, such as straw and grass.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p310#14/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p310#14/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p310#14/r1.claim: The water brings out grain, such as wheat and barley, and vegetation such as pasture.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r7.claim: The passage begins with grain because it is the staple food; نبات broadly includes all growth, including grain.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r4.claim: God uses abundant, beneficial rain to grow grain stored for people and livestock, edible fresh plants, and gardens with varied fruits, colors, flavors, and scents.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r11.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r11.claim: The sky, earth, rain, and plants resemble a reproductive pair: sky is male, earth female, water semen, and vegetation their offspring; springs and pools are implied.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r12.speaker: مقاتل
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r12.claim: Muqātil says every sign just mentioned is more astonishing than resurrection.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r8.claim: Rain brings out staple grains first, such as wheat and barley, then other vegetation for enjoyment and animal fodder.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p11/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p11/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p11/r1.claim: The early authorities take the water to be the direct means of bringing forth crops; Ashʿaris say they come into being at the water's presence.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p11/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p11/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p11/r2.claim: The grain and vegetation are staple crops for people and fodder; grain is named first despite later sprouting because it is more noble and usually human food.

ELMALILI:78:14-30/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:78:14-30/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:78:14-30/r2.claim: The phrase explains the purpose or consequence of sending rain; lam marks consequence and bi marks causation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r1.claim: ‘Bring forth’ rather than ‘grow’ portrays resurrection from the earth as the passage's main point; in Qaf, where favor is foregrounded, growth comes first and resurrection follows as an inference.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r2.claim: Grain is a collective for edible seeds, including wheat, barley, millet, corn, rice, and pulses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p26/r3.claim: Nabat is originally a verbal noun, then a conventional noun for useful vegetation whose seeds are not eaten, such as straw, clover, and grass.

TABATABAI:78:9-16/r12.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:78:9-16/r12.speaker: author
TABATABAI:78:9-16/r12.claim: The water brings forth grain and vegetation that provide food for people and other animals.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r1.claim: Paired with al-Mursalat, this surah uses divine providence in the heavens and earth to establish Judgment as the necessary end of a purposeful world, rewarding the God-fearing and punishing rebels.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r2.claim: The surahs share an affirmative-question style aimed at deniers; each verse reproaches them while believers' glad tidings are understood against the warning.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r4.claim: The signs of providence, mercy, wisdom, and power throughout earth and heavens show that humanity is not unchecked or unaccountable; its fixed day of reckoning must arrive.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r5.claim: Rain produces grain for people, grass and vegetation for cattle, and luxuriant orchards.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:78:12/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:78:12/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:78:12/r1.claim: The seven firm heavens, sun, rain-bearing clouds, and life-sustaining growth display God's power to create a new realm, the afterlife.

STUDYQURAN:78:15/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:78:15/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:78:15/r1.claim: God remains the primary cause: rain is the means by which He produces grain, plants, and gardens, since He made every living thing from water.
